{{Short description|Pseudolines arranged largely to study arrangements of lines}}

[[File:Wiring diagram.svg|thumb|Wiring diagram for an arrangement of pseudolines]]

[[File:Pappos pseudo.svg|thumb|upright=0.7|Pseudoline arrangement constructed by Friedrich Levi which cannot be straightened due to its violation of  [[Pappus's hexagon theorem]]<ref name="Felsner"/>]]

An '''arrangement of pseudolines''' is a family of [[curve]]s that share similar [[topology|topological]] properties with a [[arrangement of lines|line arrangement]].<ref name = "A&S">
{{citation
 | last = Grünbaum | first = B. | author-link = Branko Grünbaum
 | location = Providence, R.I.
 | publisher = American Mathematical Society
 | series = Regional Conference Series in Mathematics
 | title = Arrangements and Spreads
 | volume = 10
 | page = 40
 | year = 1972}}</ref><ref>
{{citation
 | last1 = Agarwal
 | first1 = P. K.
 | author1-link = Pankaj K. Agarwal
 | last2 = Sharir
 | first2 = M.
 | author2-link = Micha Sharir
 | contribution = Pseudo-line arrangements: duality, algorithms, and applications
 | location = San Francisco
 | pages = 800–809
 | publisher = Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics
 | title = Proc. 13th ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA '02)
 | contribution-url = http://portal.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=545486
 | year = 2002
 | title-link = Symposium on Discrete Algorithms
 }}</ref> 
Most commonly, in the study of [[arrangement of lines|arrangements of lines]], these have the simple property that each crosses every other line exactly once. These can be defined in the [[projective plane]] as [[simple closed curve]]s any two of which meet in a single crossing point.<ref name = "A&S"/><ref>
{{citation
 | last1 = Eppstein | first1 = D. | author1-link = David Eppstein
 | last2 = Falmagne | first2 = J.-Cl. | author2-link = Jean-Claude Falmagne
 | last3 = Ovchinnikov | first3 = S.
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | title = Media Theory
 | year = 2007}}
</ref> Furthermore, in a '''simple''' (or ''uniform''<ref name="Shor"/>) arrangement, along with all lines being required to cross all others, no 3 pseudolines may cross at the same point.

Every arrangement of finitely many pseudolines can be extended so that they become lines in a "spread", a type of non-Euclidean [[incidence geometry]] in which every two points of a topological plane are connected by a unique line (as in the [[Euclidean plane]]) but in which other axioms of [[Euclidean geometry]] may not apply.<ref>
{{citation
 | last1 = Goodman | first1 = Jacob E. | author1-link = Jacob E. Goodman
 | last2 = Pollack | first2 = Richard | author2-link = Richard M. Pollack
 | last3 = Wenger | first3 = Rephael
 | last4 = Zamfirescu | first4 = Tudor
 | doi = 10.1007/BF01212978
 | issue = 3
 | journal = [[Combinatorica]]
 | mr = 1305899
 | pages = 301–306
 | title = Every arrangement extends to a spread
 | volume = 14
 | year = 1994| s2cid = 42055590 }}
</ref>

A common diagram used to represent an arrangement is the '''wiring diagram''', a series of parallel lines with crossings between them drawn as an "X" in a simple crossing.<ref name='Felsner'/> When drawn this way, they can be described with notation for either the order in which each line crosses the other, the state of the orders between each crossing (or allowed groups of crossing whose orders do not matter), or as a list of pairs, each pair being the labels of 2 lines which have crossed, ordered in a given direction (usually left to right). They draw similarities to [[braid group|braids]], although without any need to keep track of which crosses atop the other, the crossings may be seen as elements of the [[Coxeter group]].

Two arrangements are said to be "related by a '''triangle-flip'''" if one of them can be transformed into the other by changing the orientation of a single triangular face, or in other words, by moving one of the three pseudolines that form the triangle across the intersection of the other two. For any two simple wiring diagrams numbered 1 through {{mvar|n}} in order, one can be transformed into the other with a sequence of these triangle-flips (and vice versa). This fact has counterparts in the terminology of ''mutations'' on [[oriented matroid]]s and Coxeter relations for reduced decomposition.<ref name="Felsner"/>

Felsner and Valtr [[mathematical proof|proved]] in 2009 that for an arrangement of <math>n</math> pseudolines, there are at most <math>2^{0.657n^2}</math> simple arrangements. This improves upon the previous [[upper bound|bounds]] of <math>2^{0.792n^2}</math> in 1992 and <math>2^{0.697n^2}</math> in 1997. <ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Felsner
 | first1 = Stefan
 | last2 = Valtr
 | first2 = Pavel
 | title = Coding and Counting Arrangements of Pseudolines
 | journal = Discrete & Computational Geometry
 | volume = 46
 | issue = 3
 | pages = 405–416
 | date = 2011
 | doi = 10.1007/s00454-011-9366-4
 | url = https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s00454-011-9366-4.pdf
 | access-date = 2025-06-19
 | publisher = Springer Science+Business Media
}}</ref> They also proved a lower bound of <math>2^{0.1887n^2}</math>, which was improved in 2024 by Kühnast et al. to <math>2^{0.2721n^2}</math> for sufficiently large <math>n</math>.<ref name="lower"/> The number of simple arrangements of {{mvar|n}} pseudolines in the projective plane with a marked cell is known up to {{mvar|n}}=13: 

1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 16, 135, 3315, 158830, 14320182, 2343203071, 691470685682, 366477801792538 {{OEIS|id=A006247}}

The growth rate for the number of line arrangements is smaller compared to that of pseudoline arrangements; while for pseudolines <math>A_n = 2^{\Theta(n^2)}</math>, for lines, <math>A_n = 2^{\Theta(n \log n)}</math>.<ref name="lower">
{{citation

 | first1 = Fernando
 | last2 = Dallant

</ref><ref name="approach"/>

== Stretchability ==
[[File:Non-approaching vs. approaching pseudolines.png|thumb|upright=0.4|''Non-approaching'' (top) vs. ''approaching'' (bottom) pseudoline arrangements]]

A pseudoline arrangement is said to be '''stretchable''' if it is combinatorially equivalent to a line arrangement, meaning that you can straighten each one while maintaining the order in which each crosses the others. Notable arrangements of pseudolines which ''cannot'' be stretched include the arrangement of 9 pseudolines constructed by Friedrich Levi which violates the [[pappus's centroid theorem|theorem of Pappus]], and a 10 pseudoline arrangement constructed to violate [[Desargues's theorem]].<ref name="Felsner">
{{cite book 
 | last1 = Felsner
 | first1 = Stefan
 | last2 = Goodman
 | first2 = Jacob E.
 | title = Handbook of Discrete and Computational Geometry
 | edition = 3rd
 | date = 2017
 | publisher = Chapman and Hall/CRC
 | chapter = Pseudoline Arrangements
 | chapter-url = https://www.csun.edu/~ctoth/Handbook/chap5.pdf
 | isbn = 9781315119601
}}
</ref> Some ''symmetric'' pseudoline arrangements are stretchable, yet ''cannot'' be stretched into a symmetric line arrangement.<ref name="Shor"/>

'''Stretchability''' is the problem of deciding for a given pseudoline arrangement if it is equivalent to a line
arrangement, and ''simple stretchability'' is the same problem but for simple arrangements.<ref name="Schaefer"/> Determining stretchability is a difficult computational task: it is [[Complete (complexity)|complete]] for the [[existential theory of the reals]] to distinguish stretchable arrangements from non-stretchable ones,<ref name="Shor">

An arrangement of '''approaching''' pseudolines is an arrangement of pseudolines where each pair of pseudolines approach each other until they cross, and then they move away from
each other. There are arrangements of pseudolines that are not realizable with approaching pseudolines, and these are thus not stretchable in general. However, not all approaching arrangements can be stretched.<ref name="approach">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Felsner
 | first1 = Stefan
 | last2 = Pilz
 | first2 = Alexander
 | last3 = Schnider
 | first3 = Patrick
 | title = Arrangements of Approaching Pseudo-Lines
 | journal = Discrete & Computational Geometry
 | volume = 67
 | issue = 2
 | pages = 380–402
 | year = 2022
 | doi = 10.1007/s00454-021-00361-w
 | url = https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s00454-021-00361-w.pdf
 | access-date = 2025-06-14
 | publisher = Springer
| pmid = 35221404
 }}</ref> Any such approaching arrangement can be transformed into any other by a series of triangle flips. In other words, approaching arrangements have a connected ''flip graph''.

== Oriented matroids ==
{{main article|oriented matroid}}
[[File:Chirotope example.svg|thumb|upright=0.7|The top arrangement has <math>\sigma(a, b, c) = +</math>, and the bottom <math>\sigma(a, b, c) = -</math>]]
Each rank-3 [[oriented matroid]] is equivalent to an arrangement of pseudolines, and each oriented matroid which is also '''uniform''' (in which the ''independent sets'' are exactly the sets containing at most ''r'' elements, for some fixed [[integer]] ''r'') is equivalent to a ''simple'' pseudoline arrangement. Tools for dealing with one form can therefore be used to analyze its equivalent form for either study.<ref name="Felsner"/>

The ''3-signotope'' or '''chirotope''' <math>\sigma</math> which corresponds to a given pseudoline arrangement is defined as follows: the sign of <math>\sigma(a, b, c)</math> for <math>a < b < c</math> describes the orientation of the triangle formed by 3 pseudolines <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, and <math>c</math>. If <math>a</math> and <math>c</math> cross ''below'' <math>b</math>, then <math>\sigma(a, b, c) = +</math>. If <math>a</math> and <math>c</math> cross ''above'' <math>b</math>, then <math>\sigma(a, b, c) = -</math>.<ref>
{{cite conference
 | title = An Extension Theorem for Signotopes
 | first1 = Helena | last1 = Bergold
 | first2 = Stefan | last2 = Felsner
 | first3 = Manfred | last3 = Scheucher
 | conference = 39th International Symposium on Computational Geometry (SoCG 2023)
 | series = Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics (LIPIcs)
 | volume = 258
 | pages = 17:1–17:16
 | year = 2023
 | publisher = Schloss Dagstuhl–Leibniz-Zentrum für Informatik
 | doi = 10.4230/LIPIcs.SoCG.2023.17
 | doi-access = free | arxiv = 2303.04079
}}
</ref> Equivalently, if <math>a</math> crosses <math>b</math> ''before'' <math>c</math>, then <math>\sigma(a, b, c) = +</math>, and if <math>a</math> crosses <math>b</math> ''after'' <math>c</math>, then <math>\sigma(a, b, c) = -</math>, assuming each pseudoline is given a direction (such as the implicit direction of each pseudoline in a wiring diagram, with each directed from left to right). If all 3 lines cross at the same point, then <math>\sigma(a, b, c) = 0</math>.

== Arrangement graphs ==
{{distinguish|text=graphs defined on permutations; see [[arrangement graph]]s}}

A '''pseudoline arrangement graph''' is the [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] induced by a simple pseudoline arrangement, where vertices correspond to intersection points and edges connect vertices that are adjacent along some pseudoline. Line arrangement graphs are defined analogously for line arrangements.<ref name="BoseEverettWismath2003">{{cite journal |last1=Bose |first1=Prosenjit |last2=Everett |first2=Hazel |last3=Wismath |first3=Steve |title=Properties of arrangement graphs |journal=International Journal of Computational Geometry and Applications |volume=13 |issue=6 |year=2003 |pages=447–462 |doi=10.1142/S0218195903001281}}</ref>

Pseudoline arrangement graphs can be recognized in linear time by an algorithm that exploits their structural properties.<ref name="Eppstein2014">{{cite journal |last=Eppstein |first=David |author-link=David Eppstein |title=Drawing arrangement graphs in small grids, or how to play planarity |journal=Journal of Graph Algorithms and Applications |volume=18 |issue=2 |year=2014 |pages=211–231 |doi=10.7155/jgaa.00319 |doi-access=free|arxiv=1308.0066 }}</ref> They are 2-vertex-connected and become 3-connected when augmented with a vertex adjacent to all degree-2 and degree-3 vertices, which gives them a unique planar embedding (the "canonical embedding"). In contrast, recognizing line arrangement graphs is [[Existential theory of the reals|∃<math>\mathbb{R}</math>-complete]] (and hence [[NP-hard]]) because it requires verifying geometric realizability with straight lines (determining stretchability).<ref name="BoseEverettWismath2003" /><ref name="Schaefer" />

These graphs have several other notable combinatorial properties:<ref name="FelsnerEtAl2006">{{cite journal |last1=Felsner |first1=Stefan |last2=Hurtado |first2=Ferran |last3=Noy |first3=Marc |last4=Streinu |first4=Ileana |title=Hamiltonicity and colorings of arrangement graphs |journal=Discrete Applied Mathematics |volume=154 |issue=17 |year=2006 |pages=2470–2483 |doi=10.1016/j.dam.2006.04.006 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="DasRaoSahoo2021">{{cite conference |last1=Das |first1=Sandip |last2=Rao |first2=Siddani Bhaskara |last3=Sahoo |first3=Uma kant |title=On Degree Sequences and Eccentricities in Pseudoline Arrangement Graphs |book-title=Algorithms and Discrete Applied Mathematics (CALDAM 2021) |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=12601 |year=2021 |pages=259–271 |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-67899-9_20}}</ref>

*They are [[Graph coloring|4-edge-colorable]] and [[Graph coloring|3-vertex-colorable]]
*The [[Distance (graph theory)|diameter]] on <math>n</math> pseudolines is exactly <math>n - 2</math>, independent of structure
*A vertex is diametrical if and only if it lies on the outer face
*Their [[degree sequence]]s are completely characterized: realizable sequences have the form <math>\langle 4^{d_4}, 3^{d_3}, 2^{d_2} \rangle</math> with <math>3 \leq d_2 \leq n</math>, <math>d_3 = 2(n - d_2)</math>, and <math>d_4 = n(n-5)/2 + d_2</math>; when <math>d_2 = n</math>, then <math>n</math> must be odd
*Not all are Hamiltonian,<ref name="BoseEverettWismath2003" /> though spherical arrangement graphs always are<ref name="FelsnerEtAl2006" />

Every <math>n</math>-vertex pseudoline arrangement graph can be drawn in linear time in a grid of area <math>O(n^{7/6})</math>.<ref name="Eppstein2014" /> The width depends on the maximum [[k-set (geometry)|k-level complexity]] of pseudoline arrangements, a major open problem in discrete geometry. These graphs also admit [[universal point set]]s of size <math>O(n \log n)</math>, much smaller than the quadratic bound for general planar graphs.<ref name="Eppstein2014" /> Drawing arrangement graphs is the main task in the [[Planarity|Planarity puzzle]].<ref name="Eppstein2014" />

== Kobon triangle problem ==
{{main article|Kobon triangle problem}}

[[File:Optimal Arrangement of 19 lines for the Kobon Triangle Problem.svg|thumb|An arrangement of 19 lines forming the highest possible number of triangles (107)]]

The [[Kobon triangle problem]] is an [[open problem|unsolved problem]] in [[combinatorial geometry]] first stated by [[Kobon Fujimura]] (1903-1983). The problem asks for the largest number <math>N(k)</math> of nonoverlapping triangles whose sides lie on an [[arrangement of lines|arrangement of {{mvar|k}} lines]].

The line arrangement problem is often broken down into two parts: the equivalent problem but with pseudoline arrangements, and the problem of the stretchability of the arrangements that have an optimal triangle count. This allows pure [[combinatorics]] and [[group theory]] to be leveraged without needing to worry about violating rules like the [[theorem of Pappus]] or [[Desargues's theorem]].<ref name="Felsner"/><ref name="Bartholdi">{{citation
